knownFor: Bishop of Constantinople from 428, who taught that Christ is God and man, the two natures kept distinct and worshiped as one Christ, and who would not simply call Mary Mother of God. A council at Ephesus in 431, led by Cyril of Alexandria, judged that his teaching split Christ in two and removed him from office; he denied it and died in exile. His defense, written in Greek near the end of his life under the name of Heracleides, survives only in Syriac, kept by the Church of the East.
datesNote: Ordained bishop of Constantinople on 10 April 428; removed from office at Ephesus in June 431. The editors of his book date the emperor's order to burn his writings to August 435 and his banishment to 436. He was still living in Egypt in 439, when Socrates wrote. When and where he died is not known; Nau reckons about June 451, from stories that he died as he set out for Chalcedon. The editors of his book think he wrote it in 451 or 452
placeNote: A native of Germanicia; brought from Antioch to Constantinople in 428; after Ephesus allowed, at his own request, to retire to his monastery outside Antioch, said to be that of Euprepius; banished to the Oasis in Egypt, then taken to Panopolis, toward Elephantine, and back
role: Bishop of Constantinople, 428 to 431; preacher; author of a late defense

keyWorks.title: Sermons at Constantinople
keyWorks.about: kept only in fragments by his opponents, in Greek (edited by Loofs) and in the Latin of Marius Mercator. In one he says he honors the man who is seen for the sake of the God hidden in him, and that he separates the natures but unites the worship

keyWorks.title: Letters from exile
keyWorks.about: two letters to the governor of the Thebaid, kept by the historian Evagrius, who reads his sufferings as God's vengeance. In them the Oasis falls to desert raiders and he is let go; at Panopolis he shows himself in public; and soldiers drag him toward Elephantine and back, worn, sick and old, with a mangled hand and side

keyWorks.title: The Book of Heracleides (the Bazaar of Heracleides)
keyWorks.about: his defense, written in Greek in exile and lost in that language; it survives only in Syriac. Its Syriac translator says the writer took the name of Heracleides, a man who lived near Damascus, because his own name was hated, and that he set the book as a judge between himself and Cyril, each speaking in his own defense. In it he tells how he offered the title Mother of Christ; says Christ is immortal and unable to suffer as God, mortal and able to suffer as man; praises Leo of Rome while saying Leo agreed to his condemnation unheard; offers his own name to the church's curse if they will say of God what he asks; and ends by bidding the desert rejoice for him

traces: The emperor's law of 435 ordered his books sought out and publicly burned, and the editors of his book add that his followers' meetings were forbidden. His Greek is lost; only a few sermons and letters survive in Greek and Latin.

The Church of the East put his last book into Syriac: about 535 under the patriarch Paul, according to Bedjan; between 525 and 533 under the catholicos Maraba, Bethune-Baker conjectures, with no certainty; after 638, one editor's note allows, if the name Aleppo is the translator's own.

One mutilated copy is left, in the library of the patriarch of the Church of the East at Kotchanes in Kurdistan. It was damaged in 1843, chiefly by Kurds, in the massacre of Christians by Bedr Khan Bey. Two German scholars noticed it in the 1890s, and in 1910 Bedjan published the Syriac in Leipzig and Nau the French in Paris.

Badger reported in 1852 that the Church of the East kept three liturgies, among them the Liturgy of Nestorius, directed to be used five times a year. Abdisho's catalogue of 1298 says he wrote a large liturgy, translated into Syriac by Thomas and Mar Awa.
The rites of the Church of the East name him: the ordination rite calls him Mar Nestorius the persecuted martyr, and a marriage rite names him as one whom the enemy strove to hinder.
remembered: Narsai, a teacher of the Church of the East at Nisibis who died about 503, says that the priest at the liturgy makes mention of all these before God, imitating Mar Nestorius in his supplication.
About 680 the catholicos George I wrote that the faith he set out was not the invention of Nestorius and Theodore, whom the multitude of the impious slander and whose names scandalize the simple.

In 1298 Abdisho, Nestorian metropolitan of Nisibis, wrote that the Easterns were unjustly called Nestorians, since Nestorius was not their patriarch and they did not understand his language; they held the faith in two natures already, he says, so that Nestorius followed them and not they him, and when called on to cut him off they refused.

Barhadbeshabba, about 600, told his exile as a saint's life: called back, Nestorius refuses and says the desert pleases him; brought by force, he goes to Christ on a litter. A legend, as Nau's note on a neighboring story calls it.
In the empire, Evagrius, a hostile historian of the late sixth century, writes that he learned from a writer on his death that Nestorius's tongue had been eaten through with worms.

uncertain: What he really taught is contested. Cyril and the council of Ephesus judged that his teaching split Christ in two; he denied it, saying that Christ is God and man in two natures and one Christ. Socrates, who read his writings, says he was an unlearned man who did not deny that Christ was God, and that he was scared of the word Theotokos as though it were some terrible phantom. A 1908 study by Bethune-Baker reopened the question.

Who began the quarrel over Mary's name. Socrates says his priest Anastasius, whom he had brought from Antioch, preached against the title Theotokos and Nestorius backed him and rejected it outright. Nestorius says in his book that he found two parties, one for Mother of God and one for Mother of man, who differed only in name, and offered them Mother of Christ. Evagrius's summary follows Nestorius; Hefele sides with Socrates.

The recantation. Socrates alone says that, as communion broke apart, he cried out that Mary might be called Theotokos if they wished, but no notice was taken. No other witness tells it, and bitter regret is Socrates's own reading.

When his book was written and put into Syriac. The editors reckon from references to later events that he wrote it in 451 or 452, though they note that he seems not to know the decisions of Chalcedon. The Syriac date is Bedjan's about 535, Bethune-Baker's 525 to 533 as a conjecture, or later than 638 on one editor's reading of the name Aleppo. Bazaar is held to be the translator's slip for a Greek word meaning treatise.

When and how he died. Hefele says it is unknown. Nau reckons about June 451 from stories that he died on his way to Chalcedon. Evagrius has worms from hearsay; Barhadbeshabba has a litter, in a legendary telling. Any date is Inferential-Thin; about 451 is the dominant modern reconstruction.
Who held him captive. His letter says barbarians and nomads, with the Mazices coming after; Evagrius's summary names the Blemmyes.

His own letters come to us through Evagrius, a hostile later writer, and his last book through a translator who calls Cyril impious. The brief's modern English for the book's words follows Driver and Hodgson's English, checked against Nau's French; the Syriac is not held. The sermon's modern English follows the Greek, which the Library's text gives with damaged letters.

briefReferences: Bazaar of Heracleides, translator's preface (Driver and Hodgson 2264-2289; Nau 1451-1462): the book's name, the man of Damascus, the hated name, and the translator's account of why the writer took his name.

Socrates, Church History VII.29: sent for from Antioch, a native of Germanicia, ordained 10 April 428; the first sermon, the emperor asked for the earth purged of heretics; the Arian chapel, set on fire by the Arians themselves. VII.31: he prevailed on the emperor to take away the Macedonians' churches.

Socrates VII.32: the priest Anastasius preaches against the title Theotokos, and Nestorius backs him and rejects it; Socrates's verdict that he did not deny the divinity of Christ, and the word scared as though it were some terrible phantom.
Bazaar of Heracleides (Driver and Hodgson 6915-6962): the two parties for Mother of God and Mother of man, and the title Mother of Christ offered to both.
Loofs, Nestoriana (14309-14312): his Greek sermon, I separate the natures but I unite the worship, kept by those who wrote against him.
Socrates VII.34: the party of Cyril, as a council, finds his sermons blasphemous and deposes him.

Codex Theodosianus XVI.5.66 (88695-88735): the emperor's law that his books be sought out and burned, dated to Theodosius's fifteenth consulship, 435. The editors' chronology (Driver and Hodgson 264-281, 1370-1376): the edict of August 435, banishment in 436.
Evagrius, Church History I.7: his letters to the governor of the Thebaid, the Oasis, desert raiders, the forced journey from Panopolis toward Elephantine, a mangled hand and side.

Bazaar of Heracleides, the editors on the date of writing (Driver and Hodgson 314-327): written in 451 or 452. Leo praised, yet said to have agreed to his condemnation unheard (20465-20475, 20689-20691). His name offered to the curse (20262-20266). The end of the book (20696-20703, 20731-20732): the desert, and the land of his exile as his mother who will guard his body.

Driver and Hodgson 328-333, 358-380: the Syriac translation and its date, the one damaged manuscript at Kotchanes. Their note 334-345 and 358-361: noticed in the 1890s; Syriac text and French translation of 1910.

Badger, The Nestorians and their Rituals II: the ordination rite (16355-16361), Mar Nestorius the persecuted martyr; Abdisho's The Jewel, 1298 (18315-18318, 19147-19162), Nestorius followed them and not they him.
World census, Church of the East under Persia: its tradition, and the name Nestorian fixed on it by its opponents.
